There are some big issues around electricity costs in Britain - some of them linked to net zero, some of them linked to gas, many of them bound up in decisions taken over a long period of time.
Just pointing at one bit of the problem isn’t going to help us fix them.

It DOES mention the trope around the UK accounting for less than 1% of global emissions - so we’re exempt from doing anything about it?

Won’t Britain’s successful professional services industry be able to export the know-how of running a low carbon grid (including learning from mistakes)?

It doesn’t mention that many European countries subsidise their industrial electricity use heavily - nor that GB also subsidises some heavy energy users.

Nor does it mention that large manufacturers in Britain pay far below the headline rate in those IEA figures.

It doesn’t mention that GB is less connected into the European electricity market.

It doesn’t mention that renewables have already brought down wholesale costs.

It doesn’t mention that the higher cost of capital has hit the energy industry, and that all new generation is expensive now.

It doesn’t mention that the GB grid was due an upgrade, and that the investments we make now will have a lasting payoff.

It doesn’t mention the importance of increasing electricity demand to spread the costs of that investment - nor that this increased demand is the biggest part of net zero.

It doesn’t mention the historically high share of costs levied on the electricity bill and not on the gas bill (which this govt is now addressing for households). Our European neighbours generally add taxes to gas more than electricity, which makes their electricity cheaper

This is a frustrating column by Martin Wolf - which is sadly typical of a lot of economics commentary on GB energy.

It does identify some of the key causes of high electricity prices - including Britain’s high exposure to gas prices and rising network costs. But there’s a lot it leaves out…
